concepts.def: Differences in traits between individual organisms. Variation is a defining feature of life: no two individuals, not even identical twins or members of a clone, are identical in all their traits, because genetic differences (mutation, recombination) and environmental influences both act on every organism. The patterns of variation are complex, with many traits varying independently, and these patterns are the basis on which organisms are named and classified.

The original concept of a species, as used by Linnaeus: a species is a group of organisms that share a set of traits (morphology, meaning form and structure) that distinguish them from other groups. It is still the practical basis for identifying most organisms, but it gives no rule for how much difference counts as a separate species, and it can be misled by variation within a species (for example between males and females) or by close resemblance between different species.

The two-part system of naming species introduced by Linnaeus. The first part of the name is the genus and the second part distinguishes the species within that genus, so Panthera leo (lion) and Panthera tigris (tiger) are two species in the same genus. The genus name is given an initial capital letter, the species name is lowercase, and the whole name is written in italics (or underlined when handwritten). Because the second part is only meaningful together with the genus, the same species word can be used in different genera.

A group of closely related species that share similar traits, named by the first part of the binomial. Species in the same genus, such as Panthera leo and Panthera tigris, resemble one another more closely than species in different genera, but they remain separate species.

The definition of a species as a group of organisms that can breed with one another and produce fertile offspring. Two populations belong to different species if they cannot interbreed, or if they interbreed but produce only infertile offspring. It is one of several competing species concepts and has known challenges: it cannot be applied to fossils, to organisms that reproduce only asexually, or to populations that are separated geographically and so never have the chance to interbreed, and hybridization between recognized species sometimes produces fertile offspring.

An offspring produced when members of two different species breed. Under the biological species concept the test is whether the hybrid is fertile: a mule, produced by a horse and a donkey, is infertile, so horse and donkey remain separate species even though they can breed together.

The splitting of one species into two or more species. It usually happens gradually rather than by a single act: populations that stop interbreeding accumulate differences in their traits over many generations, and at some point they are regarded as different species. Because the divergence is continuous, there is no precise moment at which speciation is complete.

A group of organisms of the same species living in the same area at the same time, and so able to interbreed. A species may consist of many populations; when populations stop interbreeding and diverge, it can become an arbitrary decision whether they are still populations of one species or have become separate species.

The number of chromosomes in a body cell of a species, in which chromosomes are present in homologous pairs (one of each pair from each parent). It is an even number in a diploid cell because the chromosomes come in pairs. Chromosome numbers vary widely between plant and animal species and are not a measure of complexity: humans have 46 chromosomes and chimpanzees have 48.

The number and appearance of the chromosomes in the cells of an organism, described by chromosome number, and by the length, centromere position and banding pattern of each chromosome. Karyotyping is the process of finding an organism's karyotype, usually from cells arrested in metaphase of mitosis when the chromosomes are condensed and visible.

An image in which the chromosomes from one cell, photographed at metaphase, have been cut out and arranged in homologous pairs in a standard order, usually by decreasing length, with the sex chromosomes last. Homologous chromosomes are matched by their length, the position of the centromere and the pattern of bands produced by staining, so that a pair cannot be matched on length alone.

The hypothesis that human chromosome 2 arose by end-to-end fusion of two chromosomes that were separate in the shared ancestor of humans and chimpanzees (the two chromosomes that were numbered 12 and 13 in the chimpanzee, now called 2A and 2B), which explains why humans have 46 chromosomes while chimpanzees have 48. Its predictions can be tested: human chromosome 2 should carry telomere-like sequences near its middle, a second (inactive) centromere region, and banding patterns that match the two chimpanzee chromosomes laid end to end. It is therefore a testable hypothesis.

A proposed explanation from which predictions can be derived and checked against observations or experiments, so that the hypothesis could in principle be shown to be false. The origin of chromosome 2 by fusion is testable because it predicts specific, observable sequence and banding features. A statement that makes no checkable prediction, or that concerns values or preferences rather than the natural world, is non-testable and lies outside what science can decide.

All the genetic information of an organism: the complete base sequence of its DNA, including genes and non-coding regions, in the nucleus and in mitochondria and chloroplasts. Organisms of the same species share most of their genome, but no two individuals (other than clones) have identical genomes.

A position in the genome at which a single base differs between individuals of the same species. SNPs are the commonest source of genome diversity within a species; most fall in non-coding DNA or do not change the amino acid coded for, so they need not affect the phenotype, although some do.

The total amount of DNA in one copy of an organism's genome, measured in base pairs (or picograms of DNA). Eukaryote genomes vary enormously in size, and this variation is not a simple reflection of the number of genes or of the organism's complexity, because much of the DNA in a large genome is non-coding or repetitive. Genomes also vary in base sequence, and the differences between species are much larger than the differences between individuals within a species.

An online database, such as the Animal Genome Size Database or the NCBI Genome resource, from which the genome size of species in different taxonomic groups can be extracted for comparison. Comparing the values shows that genome size does not increase in step with organism complexity: some amphibians and flowering plants have genomes tens of times larger than the human genome.

Determining the complete base sequence of an organism's DNA. Its speed has increased and its cost has fallen dramatically: the first human genome took over a decade and a project budget of around three billion dollars, whereas a human genome can now be sequenced in about a day for a few hundred dollars. Current uses include research into evolutionary relationships by comparing the genomes of different species; a potential future use is personalized medicine.

A potential future use of whole genome sequencing in which a person's own genome sequence is used to guide their medical care, for example predicting their risk of particular diseases, choosing the drug and dose most likely to work for them, or matching a cancer treatment to the mutations in their tumour. It is a probabilistic tool, because for most diseases the genome affects risk rather than determining the outcome.

The movement of genetic material between organisms other than from parent to offspring, for example the transfer of plasmid DNA between bacteria, including between bacteria of different species. Because genes can pass between species, bacterial species do not have the sealed gene pools that the biological species concept assumes.

concepts.term: Asexual reproduction and the species concept
concepts.def: Organisms that reproduce only asexually (for example many bacteria, and some plants, fungi and animals such as bdelloid rotifers) produce offspring genetically identical to the parent without breeding, so the test of whether they can breed and produce fertile offspring cannot be applied. Their species are defined instead on morphological, ecological or genetic (DNA sequence) similarity.

concepts.term: Chromosome number as a shared trait
concepts.def: All members of a species normally have the same number of chromosomes, so chromosome number is a trait shared within a species. Closely related species can have different numbers, and cross-breeding between them is unlikely to produce fertile offspring, because the hybrid inherits an unequal set of chromosomes from its two parents and these cannot form homologous pairs in meiosis, so viable gametes are not made. A horse (64 chromosomes) and a donkey (62) produce a mule with 63 chromosomes, which is almost always sterile.

An identification tool consisting of a series of numbered steps, each offering exactly two contrasting choices based on a trait that is fixed and easily observed, with each choice leading either to the name of an organism or to another step. A good key uses traits that do not vary with age, season or the individual (such as leaf arrangement or the number of legs) rather than variable traits such as size or colour, and is built by engaging with the local plant or animal species it is meant to identify.

A short, standardized section of DNA, sequenced from a sample, whose base sequence identifies the species it came from by comparison with a reference database. Different regions are used for different groups, for example part of the mitochondrial COI gene for animals and chloroplast genes such as rbcL and matK for plants. A barcode is not the whole genome: it is a region that varies enough between species, but little enough within a species, to serve as a label.

DNA collected from an environmental sample such as water, soil or air, rather than from an organism itself, shed in skin cells, mucus, faeces, pollen or other material. Barcoding eDNA reveals which species have left DNA in a habitat, allowing its biodiversity to be surveyed rapidly and without capturing or seeing the organisms, although a detection shows only that DNA of the species was present in the sample, not where or when the organism itself was.

mcqs.q: Which statement best describes variation between organisms?
options: No two individuals are identical in all their traits, and the patterns of variation are the basis for classifying organisms.
Individuals produced by asexual reproduction share one genome and so are identical in all of their traits.
Organisms are classified by a single distinguishing trait, so variation in the other traits is not used in naming them.
Organisms that look markedly different from one another must be members of two different species.
mcqs.specStatementText: Variation is universal, and it is what classification is built on
mcqs.explain: Variation is a defining feature of life. No two individuals are identical in all their traits, and because many traits vary independently the patterns of variation are complex; it is these patterns that are used to name and classify organisms.
rationales: Variation is a defining feature of life. No two individuals are identical in all their traits, and because many traits vary independently the patterns of variation are complex; it is these patterns that are used to name and classify organisms.

A student who equates an identical genome with an identical organism picks this. Members of a clone still differ, because of mutations arising in body cells, differences in gene expression and the effects of the environment; no two individuals are identical in all their traits.

A student who sorts living things by one obvious feature picks this. The patterns of variation are complex, and classification rests on whole suites of shared traits, which is why a whale is a mammal despite living like a fish.

A student who treats visible difference as the definition of a species picks this. Large differences occur within a species, for example between males and females, so appearance alone cannot settle whether two organisms are the same species.

mcqs.q: A gardener grows 50 plants from cuttings taken from one parent plant, so all 50 have the same genome. The plants differ from one another in height and in the number of flowers they produce. What does this show?
options: The cuttings must have been taken from more than one parent plant, because the members of a clone are identical in every one of their traits.
Variation occurs between all individuals, because the environment and new mutations act on organisms even when they share a genome.
The plants must differ at many genes, since any difference in a trait requires some difference in base sequence.
Height and flower number are not traits used in classification, so these differences do not count as variation.
mcqs.specStatementText: Variation is universal, and it is what classification is built on
mcqs.explain: No two individuals are identical in all their traits, even when they start with the same genome. Differences in the environment of each plant, and any mutations arising in its cells, produce variation in height and flowering; variation is a defining feature of life.
rationales: A student who believes a clone is identical in every trait picks this. A clone shares a genome, but variation in traits still arises from the environment (light, water, soil) and from new mutations, so no two individuals are identical.

No two individuals are identical in all their traits, even when they start with the same genome. Differences in the environment of each plant, and any mutations arising in its cells, produce variation in height and flowering; variation is a defining feature of life.

A student who thinks every trait difference must be genetic, and every genetic difference must show, picks this. The plants share a genome; the differences here are mainly environmental, and most base differences between individuals have no effect on traits anyway.

A student who thinks only classifying traits count picks this. All differences in traits between individuals are variation; classification draws on the complex patterns of that variation, not on a fixed list of traits.

mcqs.q: How did Linnaeus define a species?
options: As a group that can breed to produce fertile offspring
As a group of organisms that can mate and have offspring
As a group of organisms that share a set of traits
As organisms that look identical in every trait
mcqs.specStatementText: A species as a group sharing a set of traits
mcqs.explain: Linnaeus used the original morphological concept: a species is a group of organisms with shared traits, which distinguish them from other groups. This remains the practical basis of identification.
rationales: A student who thinks there is one definition of a species and that it is the biological species concept picks this. That concept came much later; Linnaeus classified by shared traits, the original morphological concept, and competing definitions still exist.

A student who remembers a species as organisms that can breed together, and drops the condition of fertile offspring, picks this. It is neither Linnaeus's concept nor a correct statement of the biological species concept.
Linnaeus used the original morphological concept: a species is a group of organisms with shared traits, which distinguish them from other groups. This remains the practical basis of identification.
A student who thinks members of a species must look the same picks this. Linnaeus grouped organisms sharing a set of traits, not identical ones; individuals within a species vary, sometimes greatly.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the scientific name of the tiger, Panthera tigris, is correct?
options: The second word, tigris, is on its own enough to identify the species of tiger.
It should be written Panthera Tigris, because both of its words are proper nouns.
Panthera tigris and Panthera leo are varieties of one species and interbreed freely.
Panthera names the genus and tigris distinguishes the species within it.
mcqs.specStatementText: The two-part scientific name
mcqs.explain: In the binomial system the first part of the name identifies the genus and the second part distinguishes the species from other species in that genus. Panthera leo, the lion, shares the genus and has similar traits.
rationales: A student who treats the second word as a stand-alone species name picks this. The second part only distinguishes the species within its genus; the same species word is used in other genera, so the full binomial is needed.
A student who capitalizes both parts as if they were English proper names picks this. The genus name is given an initial capital letter but the species name is always lowercase: Panthera tigris.

A student who reads a shared genus name as a shared species picks this. Tigers and lions are separate species that share similar traits; they do not interbreed in the wild and the rare captive hybrids are not a fertile breeding population.

In the binomial system the first part of the name identifies the genus and the second part distinguishes the species from other species in that genus. Panthera leo, the lion, shares the genus and has similar traits.

mcqs.q: The lion is Panthera leo and the tiger is Panthera tigris. What can be concluded from these names alone?
options: Lions and tigers are two distinct species with similar traits that are classified together in the genus Panthera.
Lions and tigers are two varieties of a single species, Panthera, that interbreed freely in the wild.
Each species is named by its second word alone, so the shared first word carries no information about them.
Lions and tigers look so different that they cannot be closely related enough to be placed in the same genus.
mcqs.specStatementText: The two-part scientific name
mcqs.explain: Different second words mean different species; the same first word means they are placed in the same genus. Species in the same genus share similar traits because they are closely related.
rationales: Different second words mean different species; the same first word means they are placed in the same genus. Species in the same genus share similar traits because they are closely related.
A student who reads the shared first word as the species picks this. Panthera is the genus; leo and tigris are two species within it, and they do not form a single interbreeding population.
A student who thinks the species word stands alone picks this. The genus name is part of the species' name and tells you that the two species are closely related, with similar traits.

A student who judges relatedness by appearance alone picks this. The names themselves state that the two species are in one genus; genus membership rests on many shared traits, not on overall resemblance in colour or pattern.

mcqs.q: According to the biological species concept, what is a species?
options: A group of organisms that can mate and produce offspring of any kind
A group of organisms that can breed together and produce fertile offspring
A group of organisms that resemble one another in every visible trait
A group of organisms that live in the same area and interbreed with one another
mcqs.specStatementText: A species as a group that can breed and produce fertile offspring
mcqs.explain: The biological species concept defines a species as a group of organisms that can breed with one another and produce fertile offspring. Fertility of the offspring is the decisive condition.
rationales: A student who remembers the concept without the condition of fertile offspring picks this. Horses and donkeys produce mules, but mules are infertile, so horse and donkey are separate species.
The biological species concept defines a species as a group of organisms that can breed with one another and produce fertile offspring. Fertility of the offspring is the decisive condition.

A student who defines a species by appearance picks this. Resemblance is the basis of the older morphological concept, and even there identical appearance is not required; the biological concept is about interbreeding.

A student who reads 'can breed' as 'do breed' picks this. The concept concerns the ability to interbreed and produce fertile offspring, not whether populations actually meet; living in the same area describes a population, not a species.

mcqs.q: Two populations of a bird species live on islands 2000 km apart and have never been observed to meet in the wild. In captivity, birds from the two populations breed readily and produce fertile offspring. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: They are two separate species, because populations that never interbreed with each other in nature are different species by definition.
They are certainly one species, because the biological species concept is the only definition of a species that biologists accept.
By the biological species concept they are one species, though applying it to populations that never meet is a known difficulty.
They are one species because they can produce offspring; whether those offspring are fertile is not relevant.
mcqs.specStatementText: A species as a group that can breed and produce fertile offspring
mcqs.explain: The populations can breed and produce fertile offspring, so by the biological species concept they belong to one species. But populations that are separated geographically are a challenge for the concept, because their capacity to interbreed cannot normally be tested in nature, and other species concepts might judge differently.
rationales: A student who reverses the logic of speciation, treating separation itself as speciation, picks this. The biological species concept asks whether organisms can interbreed and produce fertile offspring, and these birds can.

A student who believes the biological species concept is the sole, official definition picks this. Competing species definitions exist, and geographically separated populations are a recognized difficulty for the biological concept, so certainty is not justified.

The populations can breed and produce fertile offspring, so by the biological species concept they belong to one species. But populations that are separated geographically are a challenge for the concept, because their capacity to interbreed cannot normally be tested in nature, and other species concepts might judge differently.

A student who drops the fertility condition picks this. The conclusion happens to be one species here, but the reasoning is wrong: the fertility of the offspring is exactly what the biological species concept requires.

mcqs.q: Two populations of a salamander have been separated by a river for about 10 000 years. They now differ slightly in colour, rarely interbreed where they meet, and the few hybrids are fertile. One biologist regards them as one species and another regards them as two. Why can both positions be defended?
options: Speciation happens in a single act, so one of the biologists must simply have missed the event that created the new species.
Whether two populations are one species or two is a fixed fact, so a better test is all that is needed to settle it for good.
Populations that differ in a visible trait such as colour are different species, so the first biologist is mistaken.
Speciation is gradual, so populations part-way through divergence are not clearly one species or two.
mcqs.specStatementText: Speciation is gradual, so some boundaries are arbitrary
mcqs.explain: Speciation is the splitting of one species into two or more, and it usually happens gradually with populations becoming more and more different. Part-way through, it can be an arbitrary decision whether two populations are regarded as the same or as different species.
rationales: A student who pictures speciation as an event at a branch point picks this. There is no single act to miss; the populations are diverging continuously, and that is precisely why the decision is open.

A student who expects species to be sharp, objective categories picks this. Because divergence is gradual, no test can find a boundary that does not exist yet; the decision for populations at this stage is a judgement.
A student who uses visible difference as the test of a species picks this. Slight colour differences occur within many species, and the fertile hybrids show the populations have not fully diverged.

Speciation is the splitting of one species into two or more, and it usually happens gradually with populations becoming more and more different. Part-way through, it can be an arbitrary decision whether two populations are regarded as the same or as different species.

mcqs.q: Which statement about speciation is correct?
options: It is the splitting of one species into two or more, usually happening gradually as populations become more different.
It occurs at the moment when a single mutation produces the first individual of a new species.
It ends at a definite point that can be identified by testing whether the populations are separate.
It is complete as soon as a population becomes geographically separated from the rest of its species.
mcqs.specStatementText: Speciation is gradual, so some boundaries are arbitrary
mcqs.explain: Speciation is the splitting of one species into two or more. It usually happens gradually rather than by a single act, with non-interbreeding populations becoming more and more different in their traits.
rationales: Speciation is the splitting of one species into two or more. It usually happens gradually rather than by a single act, with non-interbreeding populations becoming more and more different in their traits.
A student who models the origin of a species on the origin of a mutation picks this. Speciation is a change in populations over many generations, not the appearance of one individual.

A student who expects an objective boundary picks this. Because divergence is gradual, there is often no definite point, and whether two populations are regarded as separate species can be an arbitrary decision.

A student who equates separation with speciation picks this. Separation may start the process, but the populations must then diverge in their traits over time; a newly separated population is still the same species.

mcqs.q: Which statement about chromosome numbers is correct?
options: Humans must have more chromosomes than chimpanzees, because humans are the more complex and advanced organism.
Human diploid cells have 46 chromosomes, chimpanzee diploid cells have 48, and diploid numbers are even.
Human body cells contain 23 chromosomes in total, which is why a diploid number can be an odd number.
Chromosome number determines genome size, so 48 chromosomes must contain more DNA than 46.
mcqs.specStatementText: Chromosome numbers vary between species and are always even in diploid cells
mcqs.explain: Humans have 46 chromosomes and chimpanzees 48. A diploid cell has two sets of chromosomes, one from each parent, forming homologous pairs, so its chromosome number is even.
rationales: A student who reads chromosome number as a measure of complexity picks this. Humans have 46 chromosomes and chimpanzees 48; chromosome number varies between species and does not indicate complexity.
Humans have 46 chromosomes and chimpanzees 48. A diploid cell has two sets of chromosomes, one from each parent, forming homologous pairs, so its chromosome number is even.

A student who confuses the number of pairs with the number of chromosomes picks this. Human body cells have 23 pairs, that is 46 chromosomes; because chromosomes come in pairs, diploid numbers are even.

A student who thinks genome size is set by the number of chromosomes picks this. Genome size is the total amount of DNA; a species with fewer, longer chromosomes can have a larger genome than one with more.

mcqs.q: A student reads that a dog has 78 chromosomes in its body cells, a human 46 and a chimpanzee 48. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Dogs must be more complex organisms than humans, since they have the largest number of chromosomes.
The dog genome must contain the most DNA, because its DNA is packaged into the most chromosomes.
Chromosome number varies between species, and it does not indicate how complex a species is.
Humans have 46 pairs of chromosomes and chimpanzees 48 pairs, one set from each parent.
mcqs.specStatementText: Chromosome numbers vary between species and are always even in diploid cells
mcqs.explain: Diversity in chromosome number exists among plant and animal species. The human (46) and chimpanzee (48) example shows that the number is unrelated to complexity, and the dog's 78 shows how widely it varies.
rationales: A student who treats chromosome number as a scale of complexity picks this. Chromosome number is just the number of pieces into which the DNA is packaged and says nothing about complexity.

A student who thinks genome size follows chromosome number picks this. Genome size is the total amount of DNA, and many chromosomes can be short; the dog genome is in fact smaller than the human genome.

Diversity in chromosome number exists among plant and animal species. The human (46) and chimpanzee (48) example shows that the number is unrelated to complexity, and the dog's 78 shows how widely it varies.
A student who confuses chromosomes with pairs picks this. The numbers given are total chromosomes: humans have 23 pairs (46) and chimpanzees 24 pairs (48).

mcqs.q: Which set of features is used to classify the chromosomes when a karyogram is prepared?
options: Length only, so that chromosomes of equal size are matched into pairs
Number of genes and total amount of DNA in each chromosome
Base sequence differences, seen directly as bands on the chromosome
Length, position of the centromere, and banding pattern
mcqs.specStatementText: Karyograms, and the testable idea that chromosome 2 is a fusion
mcqs.explain: Chromosomes in a karyogram are classified by their length, by the position of the centromere, which sets the relative lengths of the two arms, and by the pattern of bands produced by staining.
rationales: A student who takes the size-ordered layout of a karyogram as the method picks this. Several different chromosomes are similar in length, so centromere position and banding pattern are also needed to match homologous pairs.

A student who measures chromosomes by gene number or DNA content picks this. Neither is visible under the microscope; chromosomes are classified by what can be seen: length, centromere position and banding pattern.

A student who thinks bands show individual base differences picks this. Bands are produced by stains binding to regions of the chromosome and are the same in every normal member of a species; they do not show single-base variation.
Chromosomes in a karyogram are classified by their length, by the position of the centromere, which sets the relative lengths of the two arms, and by the pattern of bands produced by staining.

mcqs.q: Human chromosome 2 contains telomere-like sequences near its middle and a second, inactive centromere region, and its banding pattern matches the two chimpanzee chromosomes formerly numbered 12 and 13 placed end to end. How well does this evidence support the hypothesis that chromosome 2 arose by fusion of two chromosomes in a shared primate ancestor?
options: Strongly: the fusion hypothesis predicts exactly these features, and none would be expected if a chromosome pair had simply been lost.
Weakly: the simpler explanation is that humans lost one whole chromosome pair, which requires no fused chromosome.
Not at all: the fusion happened millions of years ago, so no observation made today can test what actually occurred.
Weakly: the human genome contains less DNA than the chimpanzee genome, so DNA was lost rather than rearranged.
mcqs.specStatementText: Karyograms, and the testable idea that chromosome 2 is a fusion
mcqs.explain: Telomeres normally cap chromosome ends and each chromosome has one centromere, so internal telomere sequences and a second centromere are what an end-to-end fusion would leave behind, and the matching banding shows which chromosomes fused. The evidence fits the prediction and is hard to explain otherwise.
rationales: Telomeres normally cap chromosome ends and each chromosome has one centromere, so internal telomere sequences and a second centromere are what an end-to-end fusion would leave behind, and the matching banding shows which chromosomes fused. The evidence fits the prediction and is hard to explain otherwise.

A student who explains 46 versus 48 by subtraction picks this. Losing a whole chromosome pair would delete hundreds of genes and be lethal, and it would not explain telomere sequences and a spare centromere in the middle of chromosome 2.
A student who thinks only repeatable experiments count as tests picks this. A hypothesis about the past is testable if it makes predictions about present evidence, and this one does.

A student who thinks fewer chromosomes must mean less DNA picks this. Chromosome number does not set genome size; fusion repackages the same DNA into one chromosome, and the internal telomeres and second centromere show that is what happened.

mcqs.q: A student claims: 'The fusion that formed human chromosome 2 happened too long ago to be tested scientifically.' Which response is correct?
options: The student is right: a hypothesis about a past event cannot be tested because the event itself cannot be repeated.
The hypothesis is testable, because it predicts observable features of chromosome 2 that might have been absent.
The hypothesis is testable only because most scientists have now accepted that the fusion took place.
The student is right: loss of a chromosome pair is an equally good explanation that no evidence can rule out.
mcqs.specStatementText: Karyograms, and the testable idea that chromosome 2 is a fusion
mcqs.explain: A testable hypothesis is one whose predictions can be checked and could fail. Fusion predicts internal telomere sequences, a second centromere region and matching banding; had these been absent, the hypothesis would have been rejected. Its age is irrelevant.
rationales: A student who equates testing with repeating an event in an experiment picks this. Testing means checking predictions; the fusion predicts features of chromosome 2 that can be examined today.

A testable hypothesis is one whose predictions can be checked and could fail. Fusion predicts internal telomere sequences, a second centromere region and matching banding; had these been absent, the hypothesis would have been rejected. Its age is irrelevant.
A student who confuses 'testable' with 'accepted' or 'proven' picks this. Testability depends on whether the claim makes checkable predictions, not on how many scientists believe it.

A student who thinks humans lost a chromosome pair picks this. That alternative makes its own predictions, and it fails them: loss would not leave telomere sequences and a spare centromere in the middle of a chromosome.

mcqs.q: What is meant by the genome of an organism?
options: The set of genes that is identical in every member of the organism's species
The number of chromosomes in each of the organism's diploid body cells
All of the genetic information of the organism, including non-coding DNA
The genes whose base sequences determine all of the proteins the organism makes
mcqs.specStatementText: Within a species, genomes are mostly shared but never identical
mcqs.explain: The genome is all the genetic information of an organism: the whole base sequence of its DNA, coding and non-coding, in the nucleus and in mitochondria and chloroplasts. Members of a species share most of their genome.
rationales: A student who pictures one shared blueprint per species picks this. Each individual has its own genome; members of a species share most of it, but single-nucleotide polymorphisms and other variations make every genome slightly different.
A student who confuses the genome with chromosome number picks this. Chromosome number is how the genome is packaged; the genome is the genetic information itself.

The genome is all the genetic information of an organism: the whole base sequence of its DNA, coding and non-coding, in the nucleus and in mitochondria and chloroplasts. Members of a species share most of their genome.
A student who thinks all DNA codes for protein picks this. Protein-coding genes are only a small part of a eukaryote genome; the genome includes all the non-coding DNA as well.

mcqs.q: Two unrelated people have their genomes sequenced. At one position on chromosome 7, in a region between genes, one person has T and the other has C. What is the best description of this difference?
options: A mutation that must alter a protein, so the two people will differ in some visible trait
A sequencing error, because any two members of one species must have the same genome
A variant that fixes which diseases each of the two people will develop later in life
A single-nucleotide polymorphism that is unlikely to affect either person's traits
mcqs.specStatementText: Within a species, genomes are mostly shared but never identical
mcqs.explain: A single-base difference between individuals of a species is a single-nucleotide polymorphism. Between genes it is not translated, so it is unlikely to affect either person's phenotype; SNPs like this are the main source of genome diversity within a species.
rationales: A student who thinks every base difference changes a protein picks this. The position is between genes, so it is not translated; most of the millions of SNPs between two people have no effect on the phenotype.

A student who believes all humans share one genome picks this. Members of a species share most of their genome, but any two people differ at millions of positions; this is normal within-species diversity.

A student who reads the genome deterministically picks this. A single non-coding base difference does not fix anyone's medical future; even variants that matter usually change risk rather than determine outcomes.

A single-base difference between individuals of a species is a single-nucleotide polymorphism. Between genes it is not translated, so it is unlikely to affect either person's phenotype; SNPs like this are the main source of genome diversity within a species.

mcqs.q: From a genome size database a student extracts these values: fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster) about 180 million base pairs; human about 3100 million; bread wheat about 17 000 million; the flowering plant Paris japonica about 150 000 million. What do the data show about genome size and organism complexity?
options: Genome size varies enormously and does not increase with complexity, since two plants have genomes far larger than the human genome.
Paris japonica must be the most complex organism of the four, because it has by far the largest genome of them.
Wheat and Paris japonica must have many more chromosomes than humans, since genome size depends on chromosome number.
Wheat must make about five times as many proteins as a human, because all of its extra DNA codes for protein.
mcqs.specStatementText: Comparing genome sizes across groups
mcqs.explain: The values span nearly a thousandfold, and the two largest belong to plants rather than to the most complex animal. Genome size is the total amount of DNA, much of it non-coding, and comparisons across taxonomic groups show it does not track complexity.
rationales: The values span nearly a thousandfold, and the two largest belong to plants rather than to the most complex animal. Genome size is the total amount of DNA, much of it non-coding, and comparisons across taxonomic groups show it does not track complexity.

A student who assumes a larger genome means a more complex organism picks this. Paris japonica is a small herbaceous plant; its huge genome consists mostly of repetitive non-coding DNA, not extra instructions for complexity.

A student who thinks genome size is set by chromosome number picks this. Genome size is the total amount of DNA regardless of how it is divided; both plants have fewer chromosomes than humans, packaged as much longer chromosomes.
A student who treats all DNA as protein-coding picks this. Most of a large eukaryote genome is non-coding or repetitive, so a fivefold larger genome does not mean a fivefold larger set of proteins.

mcqs.q: Which statement about whole genome sequencing is correct?
options: Sequencing a single complete human genome still takes several years and costs many hundreds of millions of dollars.
Its cost has fallen and its speed has increased, and it is used in research into evolutionary relationships.
It is used routinely to tell each patient exactly which diseases they will develop and when.
It has shown that two humans differ from each other by more than a human differs from a chimpanzee.
mcqs.specStatementText: What genome sequencing is used for now, and might be soon
mcqs.explain: Whole genome sequencing has become steadily faster and cheaper. A current use is comparing the genomes of different species to research their evolutionary relationships; a potential future use is personalized medicine.
rationales: A student who remembers the figures for the Human Genome Project as if they were current picks this. The speed of sequencing has increased and its cost has fallen enormously; a human genome now takes about a day and costs hundreds of dollars.

Whole genome sequencing has become steadily faster and cheaper. A current use is comparing the genomes of different species to research their evolutionary relationships; a potential future use is personalized medicine.

A student who believes the genome determines every outcome picks this. Personalized medicine is a potential future use, and even then a genome sequence indicates risks and suitable treatments rather than fixed outcomes.
A student misled by how varied humans look picks this. Sequencing shows the opposite: variation between species is much larger than variation within a species.

mcqs.q: A hospital proposes to sequence the whole genome of every patient diagnosed with cancer. Which is the most accurate description of what this could achieve?
options: Each patient's exact future diseases could be read straight from the sequence, so no further diagnosis would be needed.
The plan is unrealistic, because each genome would take several years to sequence and cost many millions of dollars.
Treatment could be matched to the particular mutations in each patient's tumour, a form of personalized medicine.
The sequences would all be the same, because every member of a species shares a single genome.
mcqs.specStatementText: What genome sequencing is used for now, and might be soon
mcqs.explain: Personalized medicine, a potential future use of whole genome sequencing, uses an individual's sequence to guide care, for example choosing drugs that target the specific mutations found in a tumour or that suit the patient's genotype.
rationales: A student who reads the genome as a fixed script picks this. For most diseases the genome affects risk rather than determining the outcome, and a sequence cannot replace diagnosis.

A student who still carries the Human Genome Project's timescale and cost picks this. Sequencing has become fast and cheap enough, about a day and a few hundred dollars per genome, for such use to be realistic.

Personalized medicine, a potential future use of whole genome sequencing, uses an individual's sequence to guide care, for example choosing drugs that target the specific mutations found in a tumour or that suit the patient's genotype.

A student who thinks a species has one shared genome picks this. Individuals' genomes differ at millions of positions, and tumour cells carry additional mutations, which is exactly what sequencing is meant to find.

mcqs.q: Genes for antibiotic resistance carried on a plasmid in Escherichia coli have been found with an identical base sequence in Klebsiella pneumoniae, a bacterium of a different genus. Why does this create difficulty for the biological species concept?
options: It shows the two bacteria have been breeding together, so they must be members of a single species.
Bacteria do not reproduce sexually, and so they cannot be placed in any species at all.
Both bacteria have a single chromosome, so by chromosome number they are the same species.
Genes are being transferred between species, so bacterial gene pools are not closed.
mcqs.specStatementText: Why the biological species concept fails for asexual organisms and bacteria
mcqs.explain: The biological species concept assumes genes are exchanged only within a species. Horizontal gene transfer moves genes between bacteria of different species and genera, so the concept does not work well for bacteria.
rationales: A student who treats plasmid transfer as breeding picks this. Horizontal gene transfer is not reproduction and produces no offspring, so it does not make the two bacteria one species; it shows that genes cross species boundaries.

A student who applies only the biological species concept picks this. Bacteria are placed in species using other criteria such as DNA sequence similarity; the difficulty is that genes cross between those species.

A student who uses chromosome number as a test of species identity picks this. Most bacteria have one chromosome; a shared number does not make two organisms one species, and it is irrelevant to the difficulty raised here.

The biological species concept assumes genes are exchanged only within a species. Horizontal gene transfer moves genes between bacteria of different species and genera, so the concept does not work well for bacteria.

mcqs.q: A horse has 64 chromosomes in its body cells and a donkey has 62. They can mate to produce a mule. Which statement correctly explains why mules are almost always sterile?
options: The mule's 63 chromosomes cannot all form homologous pairs in meiosis, so viable gametes are rarely produced.
The mule's body cells cannot complete mitosis, because an odd number of chromosomes cannot be split equally.
Horses and donkeys are one species because they produce offspring, so the mule is not a hybrid at all.
A mule has 63 chromosomes, a number found in no species, so it belongs to no species and so cannot breed.
mcqs.specStatementText: Chromosome number is shared within a species
mcqs.explain: The mule receives 32 chromosomes from the horse and 31 from the donkey, giving 63. Meiosis requires homologous chromosomes to pair, and with unequal parental sets many have no partner, so gametes almost never form; this is why cross-breeding between species with different chromosome numbers is unlikely to give fertile offspring.
rationales: The mule receives 32 chromosomes from the horse and 31 from the donkey, giving 63. Meiosis requires homologous chromosomes to pair, and with unequal parental sets many have no partner, so gametes almost never form; this is why cross-breeding between species with different chromosome numbers is unlikely to give fertile offspring.

A student who confuses mitosis with meiosis picks this. Mitosis copies each chromosome and separates the copies, so 63 chromosomes are handled without difficulty, which is why a mule grows normally; it is meiosis that fails.

A student who drops the fertility condition from the biological species concept picks this. Horse and donkey are separate species precisely because their offspring is infertile, and their different chromosome numbers are a shared trait that separates them.
A student who treats chromosome number as the definition of a species picks this. The mule is sterile because its chromosomes cannot pair in meiosis, not because of which species its number matches.

mcqs.q: A student is constructing a dichotomous key to identify five species of tree growing in a local park. Which first step is the best design?
options: 1a Tree more than 10 m tall, go to 2; 1b Tree less than 10 m tall, go to 4
1a Leaves arranged in opposite pairs, go to 2; 1b Leaves arranged alternately, go to 4
1a Leaves needle-like, species A; 1b Leaves broad, species B; 1c Leaves scaly, species C
1a Grows in the damp part of the park, go to 2; 1b Grows in the dry part, go to 4
mcqs.specStatementText: Building a dichotomous key for local species
mcqs.explain: Leaf arrangement is a fixed trait, present in every individual of a species regardless of age or season and easily observed, and the step offers exactly two contrasting alternatives, each leading to a further step.
rationales: A student who uses the most obvious difference between the specimens in front of them picks this. Height varies with age, so a young tree of a tall species would be sent down the wrong branch of the key.

Leaf arrangement is a fixed trait, present in every individual of a species regardless of age or season and easily observed, and the step offers exactly two contrasting alternatives, each leading to a further step.

A student who wants to reach answers quickly picks this. A dichotomous key offers exactly two alternatives at each step; three choices at one step is not dichotomous, and it also cannot deal with the remaining species.
A student who classifies organisms by one circumstantial feature picks this. Where a tree happens to be growing is not a trait of the organism, and the same species may grow in both places.

mcqs.q: Water samples from a pond were filtered, the DNA in them was extracted, and a barcode region was sequenced. Sequences matching the reference barcode of the great crested newt were found, although no newts were seen during the survey. Which is the best interpretation?
options: A living newt was certainly present at the exact spot and time of sampling, since eDNA occurs only where the organism is.
The result is unreliable, because only a short region of DNA was sequenced, rather than the complete genome of the newt species.
Newts probably use the pond, because eDNA barcoding is a sensitive method, though the DNA could have been carried in.
The match could be to any amphibian, because different species share most of their genome and cannot be told apart.
mcqs.specStatementText: Reading a habitat's species from environmental DNA
mcqs.explain: Barcoding environmental DNA allows the biodiversity of a habitat to be surveyed rapidly and detects species that are not seen. A match is good evidence that newts have been in the pond, with the caveat that shed DNA can persist and be transported.
rationales: A student who equates DNA with the organism picks this. Environmental DNA persists for days or weeks and can be moved by water or carried by other animals, so a detection does not fix where or when a newt was present.

A student who thinks identification needs the whole genome picks this. A barcode is a short standardized region chosen because it differs between species but not within them; it is the whole basis of the method, not a weakness.

Barcoding environmental DNA allows the biodiversity of a habitat to be surveyed rapidly and detects species that are not seen. A match is good evidence that newts have been in the pond, with the caveat that shed DNA can persist and be transported.
A student who underestimates variation between species picks this. Barcode regions differ far more between species than within a species, which is what lets a sequence be assigned to one species.

mcqs.q: Five chromosomes from one metaphase spread are described. V: long, centromere near the middle, dark bands near both ends. W: long, centromere near the middle, dark bands near both ends. X: long, centromere near the middle, one dark band near one end only. Y: long, centromere near one end, dark bands near both ends. Z: short, centromere near the middle, dark bands near both ends. Which two chromosomes should be placed together as a homologous pair in the karyogram?
options: W and X, because homologous chromosomes are simply the two chromosomes that share the same length
W and Y, because their length and banding match and centromere position is not used to match homologues
W and Z, because chromosomes with the same bands carry the same genes and so must be homologous
V and W, because they match one another in length, centromere position and banding pattern
mcqs.specStatementText: Karyograms, and the testable idea that chromosome 2 is a fusion
mcqs.explain: Homologous chromosomes are matched on all three features together: length, position of the centromere and banding pattern. V and W are the only two described that agree on all three. Each of X, Y and Z matches W on two features but differs on the third, so none of them can be its homologue.
rationales: A student who takes the size-ordered layout of a karyogram as the method picks this. Length is only one of three features: W and X are the same length, but W has dark bands at both ends and X has one band at one end only, so their banding patterns differ and they are not homologous.

A student who pictures every chromosome as a symmetrical X with a central centromere picks this. Centromere position varies between chromosomes and is a classifying feature: W has its centromere near the middle and Y near one end, so they are different chromosomes despite matching in length and bands.

A student who thinks each band is a gene picks this. Bands are regions of stain uptake, not genes, and matching bands are used together with length and centromere position. Z is short and W is long, so they are different chromosomes, whatever their banding looks like.

Homologous chromosomes are matched on all three features together: length, position of the centromere and banding pattern. V and W are the only two described that agree on all three. Each of X, Y and Z matches W on two features but differs on the third, so none of them can be its homologue.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic A3.1 Diversity of organisms
